questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Implied density from population and footprint

stimulus.body: A city has 500000 people and a footprint of 100 square kilometres. A clerk claims the implied density is 500 people per square kilometre.

questions.stem: Zane reads the passage in a file note and asks whether the claim is correct.

options.text: Yes, because density is always low
Yes, because 500 is a round number
No, because density cannot be computed

questions.explanation: Five hundred thousand divided by one hundred is five thousand, not five hundred. The clerk misplaced a zero.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Compact city and its trade-off
questions.stem: Amina's file note says a compact city houses 100000 people on 10 square kilometres; what is the density?
questions.explanation: One hundred thousand divided by ten equals ten thousand people per square kilometre. The density expresses compactness.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Tools of a smart growth policy
questions.stem: Ben asks in a file note what tools a smart growth policy uses.

answer.exemplar: Smart growth uses mixed-use zoning, transit-oriented development, infill, and urban growth boundaries to curb sprawl.

questions.explanation: Smart growth tools include mixed-use zoning, transit-oriented development, infill, and growth boundaries. They aim to curb sprawl.
questions.hint: Mention mixed use and transit orientation.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Upzoning and the supply of land
questions.stem: Cara's file note says upzoning raises allowed units from 4 to 10 on a parcel; how many additional units result?
questions.explanation: Ten minus four equals six additional units. The increase comes from higher allowable density.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Lot yield after a minimum lot size change

stimulus.body: A city reduced its minimum lot size from 1000 to 500 square metres. A developer now builds 8 houses where 4 stood before on the same site.

questions.stem: David reads the passage in a file note and asks what this illustrates.

options.misconception: confuses rule change with area change

options.text: Lot yield doubled after the rule change

questions.explanation: Reducing minimum lot size doubled yield from 4 to 8. Yield did not stay same, fall, or require more land.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Greenbelt and the land price just outside it
questions.stem: Elif asks in a file note why greenbelts affect land prices at their edge.

options.text: They increase supply inside, lowering price outside
They restrict supply inside, raising price outside
They have no effect on price

questions.explanation: Greenbelts restrict supply inside, so land just outside becomes scarcer and more expensive. Increase, no effect, or free land are wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Land price just outside a greenbelt

stimulus.body: Land just outside a greenbelt rose from 100 to 150 index points, while land inside remained undevelopable.

questions.stem: Farid reads the passage in a file note and asks what this illustrates.

options.text: The greenbelt had no price effect
The greenbelt lowered peripheral land prices
The greenbelt raised peripheral land prices

questions.explanation: The passage shows peripheral prices rising while inside land stayed undevelopable, so the greenbelt raised peripheral prices. Fall, no effect, or developability are wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Leapfrog development
questions.stem: Greta asks in a file note whether leapfrog development is efficient.

options.text: Yes, because it uses all land in order
Yes, because it avoids infrastructure costs
No, because it leaves gaps that are costly to service

questions.explanation: Leapfrog development leaves gaps that are costly to service, so it is inefficient. Contiguous use or no occurrence are wrong.

questions.subject: HUMAN_GEOGRAPHY
questions.topic: Polycentric city and why it emerges
questions.stem: Hassan's file note says a polycentric city has 3 employment centres and 120000 total jobs; if jobs are evenly split, how many jobs are in each centre?
questions.explanation: One hundred twenty thousand divided by three equals forty thousand jobs per centre. Even split gives equal shares.
